newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Asian Bank marks 30 years, but what next?.
newsitem.headline: Asian Bank marks 30 years, but what next?.

text.p: Members of the Asian Development Bank (ADB) will be celebrating 30 years of its existence when they start their annual meeting on Sunday.
But the question most will be asking is what will the next 30 years be like?
Unlike last year when delegates from the 56 member-countries haggled over how much they should pay for aid, the agenda for the meeting in Fukuoka, Japan, this year is staid.

"This is not on the agenda and I don't know whether it will be explicitly discussed but our major concern is how we can adapt ourselves to the changing environment," ADB president Mitsuo Sato told Reuters in a recent interview.
The bank, started at a time when the world was divided by ideological barriers and Asia's poorest nations were starved of capital, has found it is being pushed aside by private firms.
"Increasingly we will be marginalised and dwarfed without finding our relevance in the new environment," Sato said.
Partly because of their own budgetary problems and also because private money is now flowing across the region, traditional donors are asking why they should hand out aid.
"Many donors are saying the bank should do without any new capital injection, but borrowing countries have a different opinion," Sato said.
The ADB's aid window, called the Asian Development Fund, offers virtually interest free loans and the region's poor nations would not like to lose it.
The prospect of benefiting from this has led reclusive North Korea to seek admission as a member.
This too is not on the agenda and is likely to be discussed by officials at informal meetings.
One newspaper has reported that Japan opposed Pyongyang's membership bid, but Sato declined to comment on this.
Japan and the United States are the biggest shareholders of the bank, each holding 13.2 percent of voting rights.
The future of the Asian Development Fund itself is uncertain. At a Tokyo meeting in January, members agreed after much haggling to replenish the fund to $6.3 billion.
The money will last until the year 2000 and many donors are saying this is the last time they are contributing.
Sato thinks the ADB still has a role to play, though not purely as a lender of money.
Despite the billions of dollars from private businesses coming in, Asia is still home to the poorest people.
Businessmen will not go into areas where there are no profits, and an institution like the ADB could help by making the first few investments and thereby attracting private firms.
The bank could also advise governments on how to reform their economies, particularly financial and capital markets.
"As an international organisation with no political ambitions, the bank could also become a coordinator in world bodies," Sato said.
In April, the ADB helped the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum at a routine meeting. APEC, formed by 18 members, is potentially the world's largest trade bloc.
